title: Scientists Find 'Nightmare Fuel' Sea Spiders in the Salish Sea
summary: Imagine swimming in the Salish Sea at night and feeling tiny hairy legs creep up your body. That's the creepy picture scientists just made real! Researchers at the University of British Columbia found two brand-new species of sea spider. One has long, curved spines on its legs and striking red eyes. They named it Callipallene pilosuspedes, which means 'hairy feet' in Latin. Its mouth is triangular, split into three lips, and surrounded by wiggly tendrils — like a tiny Sarlacc pit from Star Wars. Sea spiders are ancient animals that appeared about 500 million years ago. They're related to spiders and scorpions, but they live only in the ocean. Some have as many as 12 legs! They breathe through their skin, and the males carry the eggs. The new species were collected between 2023 and 2024 during dives up to 18 meters deep. The second species, Tanystylum kiixin, is named after an old Indigenous village site. Its egg-carrying legs are small and stiff, so it can't clean itself well. These are the first new sea spider species described from the Salish Sea in almost a century. Why does it matter? Scientists say we need to know what lives in the ocean to protect it from climate change.
why_it_matters: Finding brand-new animals in ocean water near our own cities shows that nature still holds surprises, and that taking care of the sea today keeps those discoveries possible for the future.

background_read: The Salish Sea is the cold ocean water between the city of Vancouver in Canada and the state of Washington in the United States.
The University of British Columbia (a large university in Vancouver, Canada) is where the scientists who found the sea spiders work.
The 'Sarlacc pit' the scientists mentioned comes from Star Wars — it is a giant monster buried in the sand with a mouth full of wiggly tentacles.
Article_Structure: WHO: Researchers at the University of British Columbia who discovered two brand-new sea spider species.
WHAT: They described Callipallene pilosuspedes (meaning 'hairy feet'), which has curved spines and red eyes, and Tanystylum kiixin, named after an old Indigenous village site.
WHERE: In the Salish Sea, collected between 2023 and 2024 during dives as deep as 18 meters.
WHY: These are the first new sea spider species from the Salish Sea in almost a century, and knowing what lives in the ocean helps scientists protect it from climate change.

perspectives.description: They are thrilled because finding two new species in one place proves how much ocean life we still haven't discovered.
They point out that climate change could harm sea spiders and other ocean creatures before we even get to know them.
Some people find the hairy legs and wiggly mouth so strange that they joke the sea spiders are 'nightmare fuel,' even though they are harmless to humans.
